The Fees Nobody Quotes You

Product fees, valuation fees, arrangement fees, early repayment charges, settlement interest. Where they hide, and which ones you can actually negotiate.

Rates get advertised. Fees get disclosed. Those are two different verbs, and the gap between them is where a meaningful amount of money lives.

None of what follows is hidden in any unlawful sense — it's all in the paperwork, and firms are required to tell you. It's simply not in the headline, and the headline is what people compare.

On a mortgage

  • Product or arrangement fee. Often several hundred to around a thousand pounds. You can usually add it to the loan, but that means paying interest on it for the whole term, so a £999 fee added to a mortgage ends up costing considerably more than £999. This single fee is why the market-leading rate is often not the cheapest deal, and the fee analyser exists to settle that comparison on total cost.
  • Valuation fee. Sometimes free, sometimes not, and a full structural survey is a separate, much larger cost that has nothing to do with the lender.
  • Legal fees. Sometimes included on a remortgage, rarely on a purchase.
  • Early repayment charge. The big one. Typically one to five per cent of the balance if you leave during the fixed period, tapering by year. On £250,000 at three per cent that's £7,500, and it's the reason a five-year fix is a commitment rather than merely a longer deal. Read the schedule properly.
  • Exit or deeds release fee at the end, a modest but real administrative charge.
  • Higher lending charge at very high loan-to-value. Less common now, but not extinct.

On a loan or credit agreement

  • Arrangement fees. Uncommon on mainstream personal loans, more frequent at the subprime end.
  • Early settlement interest. You have a statutory right to settle early, but under the early settlement rules the lender can add up to 28 days' interest after the settlement date, and for agreements longer than twelve months, up to 30 days beyond that. That's where the "58-day rule" comes from. So settling never costs you the full remaining interest, and it never costs merely the outstanding balance either. Estimate it here before you assume paying off early is free.
  • Default and late payment fees, plus the interest that keeps accruing on top.
  • Optional insurance, priced monthly and presented as small. Worth checking whether you already have the cover through something else.

On car finance specifically

  • The balloon payment. Not a fee, but the largest number in a PCP agreement, and the one the monthly figure is designed to distract you from. See PCP versus HP.
  • Excess mileage. A small-sounding per-mile rate against a limit that's easy to exceed. The totals aren't small.
  • Return condition charges, assessed against the BVRLA fair wear and tear standard. Largely predictable, and largely avoidable if you inspect early — the damage checker walks you through the standard.
  • Option to purchase fee on HP, a small charge to actually take ownership at the end.

Which of these you can actually negotiate

More than you'd think, and it costs nothing to ask.

  • Often negotiable: mortgage product fees (there's frequently a fee-free version of the same deal at a slightly higher rate, so ask for both and compare on total cost); valuation fees; legal fees on a remortgage; car dealer admin fees.
  • Sometimes waived on request: excess mileage, if you're taking another agreement with the same finance company.
  • Rarely negotiable: early repayment charges, statutory settlement interest, Stamp Duty.

The one question that surfaces all of it. Ask, in writing: "What is the total amount I will have paid by the end of this agreement, including every fee, assuming I do nothing unusual?" A regulated firm can answer that, and the answer is directly comparable between offers in a way that a rate never is.

Where to find them before you sign

For a mortgage, the illustration or European Standardised Information Sheet lists the fees and the APRC. For a regulated credit agreement, the pre-contract information sets out the total amount payable, the APR and any charges. Both are required, both are dull, and both are the only place the real price is actually written down.

Read the total amount payable. Compare that between offers, and little else. See why that's the only number worth comparing.
